title: Memory Hog Detection
exclusions: Detects one Linux host-PID-command identity whose sampled resident set size is at least 1 GiB and whose `ps` memory percentage is at least 20 percentage points in each of three consecutive selected snapshots. It does not measure private or proportional set size, prove waste or a leak, add RSS values safely across processes, observe allocations between polls, include all kernel or cgroup memory, predict an out-of-memory kill, or establish service impact. `%MEM` is relative to host physical memory rather than a container's cgroup limit. The supplied `ps.sh` fields do not provide a reliable process-start identity, the primary SPL has no exception lookup, and this operational use case makes no compliance claim.
evidence: When deployed, retain the `linux_process_sustained_rss_hog_15m` saved-search definition, schedule and alert history, the returned host/PID/command/user and three-bucket RSS/%MEM measurements, the three underlying `sourcetype=ps` snapshots, collection-health output, and the associated incident record. These artifacts demonstrate that indexed samples met the configured candidate rule; they do not prove collection completeness, memory ownership, harmful behavior, root cause, or remediation.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index with the `Splunk_TA_nix` search-time knowledge, index three complete aligned `sourcetype=ps` table snapshots for `host=memory-hog-positive` in three adjacent closed five-minute buckets. In every snapshot include `PID=4242`, `COMMAND=memory-worker`, `USER=svc_test`, `RSS=1048576`, and `MEM=20.0`, plus at least one smaller healthy process row. Run a copy of the SPL with fixed bounds. Expect exactly one row for PID 4242 with `observed_buckets=3`, `sample_span_minutes=10`, `min_rss_mib=1024`, and `min_mem_pct=20`, proving both inclusive threshold boundaries.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run separate three-snapshot fixtures. Fixture A keeps `MEM=20.0` but uses `RSS=1048575` KiB in every bucket; fixture B keeps `RSS=1048576` KiB but uses `MEM=19.9`; both must return zero rows because one required gate is below its inclusive threshold. Fixture C uses both boundary values but omits the middle bucket and must return zero rows because persistence and the 600-second first-to-last span are incomplete. Also reuse PID 4242 with a different `COMMAND` in one bucket and confirm the identities are not bridged.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=ps` multi-line process-table snapshots produced by the `ps.sh` scripted event input supplied with the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833). The search selects the latest raw snapshot in each closed five-minute bucket before `multikv` expands its rows. Required current Linux columns are `PID`, `RSS`, `MEM`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`; documented legacy `RSZ_KB` and `pctMEM` are accepted. Linux `ps` reports RSS in KiB and memory share in percentage points. `_time` and `host` are Splunk metadata; `index=os` and the five-minute interval are deployment choices.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833), installed on Linux collection forwarders and on the Splunk tiers that require its parsing and search-time knowledge.

spl:
index=os sourcetype=ps host=* earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval snapshot_time=_time
| bin _time span=5m
| eventstats max(snapshot_time) as selected_snapshot_time by _time host
| where snapshot_time=selected_snapshot_time
| multikv
| eval process_id=trim(tostring(coalesce(PID,pid,process_id))), process_name=trim(tostring(coalesce(COMMAND,command,process_name))), process_user=trim(tostring(coalesce(USER,user,process_user,"(user unavailable)"))), rss_kib=tonumber(replace(trim(tostring(coalesce(RSS,RSZ_KB))),",","")), mem_pct=tonumber(replace(trim(tostring(coalesce(MEM,pctMEM))),"%",""))
| where match(process_id,"^[0-9]+$") AND isnotnull(process_name) AND len(process_name)>0 AND isnotnull(rss_kib) AND rss_kib>=0 AND isnotnull(mem_pct) AND mem_pct>=0 AND mem_pct<=100
| stats max(rss_kib) as rss_kib max(mem_pct) as mem_pct latest(process_user) as process_user by _time host process_id process_name
| stats count as observed_buckets min(rss_kib) as min_rss_kib avg(rss_kib) as avg_rss_kib max(rss_kib) as max_rss_kib min(mem_pct) as min_mem_pct avg(mem_pct) as avg_mem_pct max(mem_pct) as max_mem_pct earliest(_time) as first_bucket latest(_time) as last_bucket latest(process_user) as process_user by host process_id process_name
| eval required_buckets=3, required_sample_span_seconds=600, sample_span_seconds=last_bucket-first_bucket, sample_span_minutes=round(sample_span_seconds/60,1), rss_threshold_kib=1048576, rss_threshold_mib=1024, mem_threshold_pct=20
| where observed_buckets=required_buckets AND sample_span_seconds=required_sample_span_seconds AND min_rss_kib>=rss_threshold_kib AND min_mem_pct>=mem_threshold_pct
| eval min_rss_mib=round(min_rss_kib/1024,1), avg_rss_mib=round(avg_rss_kib/1024,1), max_rss_mib=round(max_rss_kib/1024,1), min_mem_pct=round(min_mem_pct,1), avg_mem_pct=round(avg_mem_pct,1), max_mem_pct=round(max_mem_pct,1)
| convert ctime(first_bucket) ctime(last_bucket)
| table first_bucket last_bucket host process_id process_name process_user min_rss_mib avg_rss_mib max_rss_mib min_mem_pct avg_mem_pct max_mem_pct observed_buckets sample_span_minutes rss_threshold_mib mem_threshold_pct
| sort 0 -min_mem_pct -min_rss_mib host process_id
description: Reports a Linux process only when the same host, numeric PID, and command has at least 1 GiB of RSS and at least 20 percent of host memory in the latest complete sample from each of three consecutive closed five-minute buckets. The result is a sustained high-residency candidate, not proof that the process is wasteful or leaking.
value: A single process that retains a large absolute and relative share of host RAM can reduce cache and workload headroom, increase reclaim or swap pressure, and precede latency or termination. Requiring both thresholds across three sampled buckets focuses response on persistent candidates while preserving the process identity and measurements needed for application, host, and cgroup-aware triage.
implementation: Enable the add-on's supplied `ps.sh` scripted event input on Linux forwarders, route complete process-table events to the deliberately selected `os` index, and collect every five minutes. Verify that `multikv` yields numeric current `RSS`/`MEM` or documented legacy `RSZ_KB`/`pctMEM` with `PID`, `COMMAND`, and `USER`. Schedule the search every five minutes on bucket boundaries; alert only when all three samples meet both the 1,024 MiB RSS and 20-percent host-memory policy gates. Treat these as tunable catalogue starting points, not Linux, procps, or Splunk defaults.
visualization: Use an active-candidates table showing host, PID, command, user, first/last bucket, minimum/average/maximum RSS MiB, minimum/average/maximum host-memory percentage, and policy thresholds. Add a drilldown line chart for the three selected samples, a separate source-freshness and parsed-row-count panel, and host/cgroup context for reclaim, swap, pressure, and OOM events. Do not sum process RSS into host usage, label RSS as private memory, or render missing samples as healthy state.
dataModelAcceleration: The add-on classifies `sourcetype=ps` as Performance data, but CIM Performance 6.4 defines host-level memory capacity and usage fields rather than per-process PID, command, RSS, or `%MEM` history. No equivalent accelerated `tstats` search is claimed. Endpoint process-start data is also not a substitute for sampled process residency, so the raw table and add-on-specific fields are required.

knownFalsePositives:
The rule identifies real sustained high RSS, but “hog” is an operational judgement. Expected or misleading matches include:

1. **Deliberately large database, search, or in-memory service** — PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch, Redis, analytics engines, and other memory-resident services may be sized to use substantial RAM. Confirm the service's approved host or workload budget, latency, reclaim, swap, and headroom before paging; baseline by service class instead of weakening the fleet rule globally.

2. **JVM heap commitment, cache warm-up, or bounded batch work** — A runtime can retain committed heap or allocator arenas after load falls, and a cache may intentionally remain hot. Compare heap-after-GC, cache hit rate, workload, application allocation telemetry, and post-idle behavior. RSS alone does not prove unreachable objects.

3. **Shared mappings and prefork workers** — RSS includes resident shared and file-backed pages, so the same pages can appear in multiple processes. Do not add process RSS to estimate host consumption. Inspect `/proc/<pid>/status` and, where authorized, `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup` for `RssAnon`, `RssFile`, `RssShmem`, and PSS before assigning ownership.

4. **Container or systemd cgroup context** — `ps` `%MEM` uses host physical memory, not `memory.max`; a process can be expected on a large host yet close to a small cgroup limit, or can match this rule while its cgroup remains healthy. Resolve `/proc/<pid>/cgroup`, then inspect cgroup v2 `memory.current`, `memory.high`, `memory.max`, `memory.events`, and `memory.stat` in bytes. Do not compare or add those values to RSS as though they measure the same scope.

5. **Service restart, PID reuse, or command truncation** — Current Linux `ps.sh` output has no process-start field and can truncate `COMMAND`. A replacement process can inherit the same PID and command across the short window. Confirm `ps ... lstart`, `/proc/<pid>/stat`, and service/deployment history before asserting one continuous process identity.

6. **Duplicate, replayed, or malformed process tables** — Duplicate input stanzas, replayed events, damaged alignment, or a locally modified script can distort fields. The SPL selects the latest raw snapshot per host and bucket and collapses duplicate identities, but raw-event and collection-health review remains required.

7. **Approved load, soak, or failover test** — A controlled exercise may intentionally hold memory. Preserve the base result, then apply an owner-approved exception keyed by exact host and stable command, active only between explicit start and end epochs and carrying reason, ticket, owner, and approver. Reject wildcards, PID-only entries, and non-expiring suppressions.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and interpretation boundary

Install a currently supported release of the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) on every Linux Universal Forwarder that will collect process snapshots. Deploy the add-on's parsing and search-time knowledge to the tiers required by the local Splunk topology, and check the current Splunkbase compatibility table before installation or upgrade. The listing warns that version 6.0 changed default indexes and configuration files, so test upgrades outside production. The operations search role needs read access to the selected operating-system index and permission to schedule this search; it does not need unrestricted Splunk administration.

Linux `ps` defines RSS as non-swapped physical memory used by a task, reported in KiB. `/proc/<pid>/status` describes `VmRSS` as `RssAnon + RssFile + RssShmem` and warns that these convenient values are not precise accounting. RSS can include shared and file-backed mappings, excludes some task-related kernel allocations, and cannot establish which application objects are live. The `MEM`/legacy `pctMEM` value is a percentage of host physical memory; it is not a percentage of a container or systemd cgroup limit. The title remains the catalogue identity, but alert text must say “sustained high-RSS candidate,” not “confirmed memory hog” or “memory leak.”

This policy requires both at least 1,048,576 KiB (1,024 MiB, exactly 1 GiB) RSS and at least 20 host-memory percentage points in every one of three selected five-minute snapshots. These are transparent, tunable starting points, not thresholds published by Linux, procps, or Splunk. The absolute gate avoids paging on a large percentage of a very small host; the relative gate avoids treating a modest allocation on a very large host as a hog. The conjunction intentionally favors precision and can miss workloads constrained by a cgroup much smaller than host RAM. Use a separately validated cgroup-capacity rule for that risk rather than changing the meaning of this process rule silently.

## Step 1 — Configure and verify process collection

Use the `ps.sh` scripted event input shipped with the add-on. On a Universal Forwarder, copy only its exact stanza from `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_nix/default/inputs.conf` into `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/Splunk_TA_nix/local/inputs.conf`; Splunk explicitly warns not to copy the whole default file because local settings persist across upgrades. Preserve the installed script path and source type, then set the local collection policy. A five-minute example is:

```ini
[script://./bin/ps.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 300
index = os
```

`interval=300` and `index=os` are this implementation's choices, not claimed product defaults. If governance selects another event index, change the input and the SPL together. Each execution emits a complete process table, so estimate indexed volume and script overhead on dense hosts before fleet rollout. Follow Splunk's documented execution-rights and operating-system privilege guidance; do not invent a modular input, HEC token, or vendor API for this local scripted source.

After deployment, inspect the effective input with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`. Search `index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-15m` and inspect `_raw`: each event must preserve a table header and aligned rows. Then run `index=os sourcetype=ps earliest=-15m | multikv | table _time host PID RSS RSZ_KB MEM pctMEM COMMAND USER`. Splunk documents that `multikv` creates a row event and derives names from the table header. Add-on version 8.7.0 changed legacy `RSZ_KB` to current `RSS` and `pctMEM` to current `MEM` while retaining backward-compatible fields; the SPL coalesces those documented pairs and treats current fields as canonical.

On a staging host, compare a collection instant with `ps -eo user:32,pid,rss,pmem,stat,lstart,comm,args --sort=pid`. Allow for script execution, forwarding, and indexing delay. Spot-check several PIDs, including the largest process, and confirm RSS units before conversion: 1,048,576 KiB divided by 1,024 is 1,024 MiB. Confirm that the extracted percentage is expressed in percentage points, not a fraction from zero to one. Record command truncation or any local `ps.sh` edit; Splunk documents a 100-character command limit in the supplied script, and changing it affects grouping and upgrade support.

## Step 2 — Save and understand the persistence search

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_process_sustained_rss_hog_15m`. Schedule it every five minutes exactly on five-minute boundaries, for example `*/5 * * * *`, and trigger when result count is greater than zero. The explicit `earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m` bounds select three closed five-minute buckets and leave one bucket for normal arrival delay. Measure actual end-to-end latency before reducing that delay. If dispatch is not aligned to five-minute boundaries, correct the schedule or redesign and retest the bounds.

The first `eval` preserves each raw event's exact timestamp as `snapshot_time`. `bin` assigns it to a five-minute bucket, and `eventstats max(snapshot_time)` runs before `multikv` so only the latest raw process table for each host and bucket is expanded. That prevents a second poll in one bucket from inflating persistence. `multikv` then creates process rows. The normalization accepts current and documented legacy fields, removes a comma from RSS and a percent sign from memory share if present, converts both to numbers, and rejects headers, missing identity, and invalid ranges.

The first `stats` creates at most one measurement per host-PID-command and bucket. The second aggregation counts the three observations and computes minimum, average, and maximum RSS and memory percentage. The final gate requires exactly three buckets, a 600-second span between the first and last bucket positions, minimum RSS of at least 1,048,576 KiB, and minimum memory share of at least 20. Using minima means every selected snapshot meets both gates; a single spike does not pass. Three samples are ten minutes apart from first to last while representing a 15-minute sampled policy. Neither phrase means the process was continuously above threshold between polls.

Identity is `host + PID + COMMAND`. It prevents different large processes on one host from being merged, but cannot fully prevent restart/PID-reuse collisions because current Linux `ps.sh` output removed `ELAPSED` and supplies no process-start value. Do not aggregate only by command, which would combine workers, or only by PID across hosts. If reliable boot ID plus process-start ticks are mandatory, build and validate a separate approved collector rather than asserting that the add-on supplies them.

The add-on maps `ps` to CIM Performance, but CIM Performance 6.4 describes host-level memory capacity and usage rather than per-process RSS, PID, and command history. No `cimSpl` is supplied because an accelerated search would change the signal. Do not map this to Endpoint `Processes.mem_usage`, fabricate a `mem_usage_percent` field, or claim data-model acceleration without a separately documented normalization and validation.

## Step 3 — Validate parsing, units, thresholds, and failure controls

Build controls as complete aligned `ps` tables with a header, because table parsing is part of the use case. For the positive boundary test, place the three snapshots from `controlTest` in adjacent closed buckets. Give PID 4242 the same command and user with `RSS=1048576` and `MEM=20.0`, and include at least one healthy row. Run a copy of the SPL against the isolated index using fixed absolute earliest/latest times. Expect one result with three observations, a 600-second span, minimum RSS 1,024 MiB, and minimum memory percentage 20. This verifies `>=` behavior and the KiB-to-MiB conversion.

Run the negative fixtures separately. One KiB below the RSS threshold must fail even when percentage is 20; 19.9 percentage points must fail even when RSS is exactly 1 GiB. A missing middle snapshot must fail the bucket-count/span gate. Reusing the PID with a different command must create separate identities, neither of which has three observations. Add malformed-row controls: replace RSS with `?`, remove the command, and use a memory percentage with nonnumeric text; each row must be rejected rather than treated as zero. Put two raw snapshots in one bucket with different timestamps and verify that only the later table is selected.

There is no Linux vendor inventory UI for this process state. Compare at least three staging collections with on-host `ps`, matching timestamp, PID, command, RSS KiB, and memory percentage. Inspect `/proc/<pid>/status` for `VmRSS`, but do not require byte-for-byte equality across different observation times or present procfs's convenient counters as exact accounting. Track source health separately with `index=os sourcetype=ps | stats latest(_time) as last_seen count by host` and a parsed-row-count trend. A quiet candidate search cannot distinguish healthy low usage from a silent or malformed collector.

This review is documentation-only. It did not execute `ps.sh`, index fixtures, run the SPL in a Splunk deployment, or validate a production platform/add-on/kernel combination. Keep `status=draft` until those controls pass and a qualified reviewer signs off. Preserve actual test outputs when validation occurs; changing status without runtime evidence would overstate assurance.

## Step 4 — Operationalize and perform host/cgroup-aware triage

Route candidates to Linux platform operations and the owning service team. Deduplicate on host, PID, and command for no more than one search interval while retaining repeated measurements. Do not automatically kill the process, restart a service, evict a workload, change a memory limit, or reboot the host. First confirm the process still exists with `ps -p <pid> -o pid,ppid,user,rss,pmem,stat,lstart,comm,args`, compare start time with the alert window, and review deployments, workload, reclaim, swap, pressure-stall data, OOM messages, and application-specific memory telemetry.

Use `/proc/<pid>/status` to separate `RssAnon`, `RssFile`, and `RssShmem`. Where permissions and policy allow, `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup` can provide proportional set size and a more useful sharing view, but access can be restricted and collection can add overhead. Runtime evidence is still needed: heap-after-GC and heap dumps for Java, allocator or object profiles for native and managed runtimes, cache statistics, or database-specific memory views. A large RSS can be efficient and intentional; a controlled restart may restore headroom but destroys diagnostics and does not repair a leak.

For a cgroup v2 workload, read `/proc/<pid>/cgroup`; the unified entry has the form `0::/<path>`, which identifies the corresponding path under the mounted cgroup hierarchy. Inspect `memory.current`, finite `memory.high` or `memory.max`, `memory.events`, and keyed `memory.stat` values. Kernel documentation states that cgroup v2 memory amounts are bytes, whereas this search's RSS input is KiB. Convert units explicitly. `memory.current` covers the cgroup's charged memory scope, not one process's RSS; `memory.max` can be the literal string `max`; `memory.high` pressure and event counters have different meanings from a hard-limit or OOM event. Never add these values to RSS or claim direct equality. Cgroup v1 uses different interfaces and needs its own runbook.

Display the candidate table, a three-point per-process chart, and independent collection-health panels. Add correlated host memory, swap, reclaim, PSI, and cgroup-limit panels only from separately validated data sources; this use case does not pretend `ps.sh` collects them. Restrict access to command arguments and raw events because command lines can expose credentials or tenant data. Label percentages as “host memory %” and all converted RSS axes as MiB so operators do not confuse percentage points, KiB, MiB, and cgroup bytes.

## Step 5 — Preserve evidence, troubleshoot, tune, and suppress safely

Retain the saved-search definition, scheduler history, result rows, three selected source snapshots, collection-health result, and incident notes according to the operations retention policy. Record threshold version, process start-time confirmation, host and cgroup context, owner conclusion, diagnostics collected, and remediation. These artifacts support operational review; they do not prove all processes were observed, establish memory ownership, or satisfy a regulatory requirement. The catalogue's 30-day hot-retention entry is an advisory planning assumption, not a mandate or statement that evidence was actually retained.

No `ps` events usually means the input remains disabled, the add-on is absent on the forwarder, execution rights or documented runtime privileges are missing, events route to another index, or the search role cannot read the index. Use `btool`, forwarder `splunkd.log`, and the add-on's script debug procedure to isolate configuration, execution, forwarding, and authorization. Raw tables without fields usually indicate a changed header, broken alignment, missing search-time knowledge, an incorrect source type, or an ingest transform that split the table. Repair extraction rather than searching arbitrary raw text or substituting undocumented fields.

If only `RSZ_KB` and `pctMEM` appear, documented backward compatibility is active and the SPL supports it. If RSS includes commas or MEM includes a percent sign, the normalization removes those characters; other locale-specific or unit-bearing values must be investigated rather than guessed. If candidates vanish intermittently, inspect per-host snapshot counts, arrival delay, PID restart history, and the latest-event selection. If indexed and on-host values differ, compare exact timestamps, namespaces, command truncation, duplicate stanzas, and whether the process changed between observations.

Baseline results by service and host class over at least one representative business cycle before changing policy. Document the owner, rationale, date, and measured effect of any threshold or interval change, and rerun the positive, negative, missing-bucket, malformed-row, and duplicate-snapshot controls. A service-specific derivative can use approved thresholds, but must preserve units, dual-gate semantics, and explicit naming so its result is not confused with the catalogue rule.

The primary SPL deliberately contains no exception lookup, making the base behavior reviewable. For a sanctioned high-memory service or test, preserve the base match and then apply a governed `linux_process_memory_exceptions.csv` lookup keyed by exact host and stable command, active only between approved start and end epochs. Require owner, reason, ticket, and approver; reject wildcards, PID-only entries, and permanent expiry. Review suppressed matches on the same cadence as alerts, and revalidate exceptions after application, kernel, host-size, cgroup-limit, or add-on changes.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for one program that keeps a very large share of a computer's working memory for several checks in a row. That gives the team a focused reason to investigate before other work runs short of room, while recognizing that a large program may be healthy and intentional.
